title: Extraction and characterization of biocompatible hydroxyapatite (Hap) from red big eye fish bone Potential for biomedica

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The method states that 2 g of bone was treated with aqueous 2 M NaOH at 250 °C for 5 h, but does not specify a sealed, pressure-rated hydrothermal/autoclave reactor. An aqueous solution cannot remain liquid at 250 °C at atmospheric pressure; water boils at 100 °C. The stated procedure is therefore physically incomplete and cannot be reproduced as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results/discussion paragraph beginning “Fig. 1 shows natural bone...”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paragraph first states that “Fig. 2 displays nanoparticles from alkaline hydrolysis of the HAp” and that alkaline hydrolysis yields “nanostructured particles,” but later says, “Based on the results, alkaline hydrolysis HAps do not contain nanoparticles.” These are directly contradictory conclusions about the same A-HAp material.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results/discussion, comparison of alkaline hydrolysis and thermal calcination
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states, “Alkaline hydrolysis produces HAp that is purer and has larger crystals than thermal calcination.” Shortly afterward it states, “Despite having larger particles than alkaline hydrolysis, thermal calcination eliminated the organic portion.” Both processes cannot simultaneously be the one with larger particles/crystals in this comparison.

The displayed Fig. 4 panels contain axes, labels, and the word “Smoothing,” but no visible FT-IR spectral traces or peaks. Consequently the figure cannot support the text's claimed bands at 1455, 1417, 1099, 1044, 963, 875, 632, 603, and 566 cm−1, nor the conclusion that organic bands are absent.

The displayed Fig. 5 consists only of panel labels “a,” “b,” and “c” and contains no plotted diffraction patterns, axes, peaks, or phase-reference information. It therefore contradicts/is incapable of substantiating the reported XRD reflections at 2θ = 25.9°, 32.2°, 39.8°, and 46.7° and the asserted crystallinity/phase-purity comparison.

The manuscript calls the 632 cm−1 HAp OH− feature an “OH bending” band and calls the 566 cm−1 phosphate feature a “phosphate stretching” mode. For hydroxyapatite, the characteristic approximately 630 cm−1 OH− feature is normally assigned to OH− libration, while approximately 560–605 cm−1 phosphate bands are ν4 O–P–O bending modes. These incorrect assignments undermine the stated spectroscopic interpretation.

predicted_errors.error_location: MG-63 MTT assay methods and abstract biological-results claim
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The method says “HAp-free cells served as the blank control.” Cells without HAp are an untreated cell control, not an MTT blank; an MTT blank should contain assay reagents/media without cells to correct non-cellular absorbance. This is especially important because particulate HAp can interfere with optical MTT measurements. No particle-only/background controls are described.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract (“proliferation rate of 92 %”) and MTT-assay description
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A single 24-h MTT endpoint, compared only with untreated cells, measures relative metabolic activity/viability, not a proliferation rate. Moreover, 92% of control is a lower signal than control, not evidence of enhanced proliferation. The text provides no initial-versus-final cell counts, time course, or proliferation-specific assay to support the proliferation claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract biological-results statements and MG-63 assay section
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper reports “92 % compared to the control” and claims “no significant adverse effects,” but gives no number of biological or technical replicates, no mean ± SD/SEM, no individual observations, no statistical test, and no p-value. Therefore the assertion of no significant effect is unsupported and the reported percentage cannot be evaluated statistically.

The manuscript describes the microscope as “SEM (JEOL JSM-5610LV Field Emission Gun)” and repeatedly labels the imaging as FESEM. The JEOL JSM-5610LV is a conventional tungsten-filament low-vacuum SEM model, not a field-emission-gun SEM. The instrument designation and the claimed FESEM characterization are inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and concluding claims of high-purity, biomedical-grade/biocompatible HAp
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: “High-purity HAp” and biomedical suitability are asserted from FT-IR, XRD, SEM, and one incomplete MTT assay. No quantitative elemental composition or Ca/P ratio, phase quantification, trace-metal analysis, residual sodium/organic analysis, endotoxin/sterility assessment, or impurity analysis is reported. FT-IR/XRD peak identification alone cannot establish high purity or biomedical-grade material.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract final sentences and results/discussion environmental claims
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper calls the process “cost-effective,” “environmentally friendly,” scalable, and a pollution-control solution without yield, mass balance, energy consumption, NaOH/acetone recovery, wastewater characterization, cost analysis, scale-up experiment, or life-cycle assessment. The described protocol includes three days of boiling, acetone use, concentrated NaOH, drying, and operation at 250 °C; these facts make the unsupported green/scalable conclusion particularly misleading.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results/discussion statement “HAp microcrystals longer than a few micrometres are seen in bone”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The statement treats micrometre-long features in raw bone as individual HAp microcrystals. Native bone mineral is nanocrystalline apatite, generally tens of nanometres in its principal dimensions; micrometre-scale SEM features would be aggregates, lamellae, or bone microstructure rather than individual HAp crystals. This conflicts with accepted bone-mineral structure and with the paper’s own nanostructure framing.
